#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""One step of the project chat against the live model, without the app.

The project chat's assistant is a system prompt (projectInstructions.ts), the
project tools and the chat. Each case here is one point in a project chat,
recorded from the real app, and the model's next step there, a tool call or a
reply, checked against one sentence of the prompt. A response may hold
several calls, and every one is judged: a change among them is the outcome
and ends the run, whatever came before it. A response of reads the case does
not decide on is answered, each read with the result the app gave for it at
the same point (recorded beside the request), and the model asked again, at
most MAX_READS times; nothing else is ever answered.

What the app sends, reproduced here:
  - instructions: rendered from projectInstructions.ts by
    tests/printer_prompt/render_prompt.mjs, so an edit to the prompt is tested
    without building anything;
  - tools: project_tools.json, the app's own tool list for the project chat
    (test_openai_responses_agent.cpp fails if it drifts from the registry);
  - input: everything else, as the app built it (requests.json). The shell
    harness's --project-prompt-requests mode plays script.json through the
    real app, with the model's outputs scripted and every tool run for real,
    and keeps the request at each point a case observes: the earlier turns as
    the app replays them, this turn's message with the workspace context, and
    this turn's calls with their live results. At the same point it calls
    the reads script.json's "answers" lists (workspace_inspect, slice_report,
    printer_list, object_analyze for each object, settings_get of every
    setting of the print, the first object, the filament and the printer,
    the filament's and printer's names asked under the print scope, a
    hand-kept list of other slicers' names, and settings_search for common
    queries) and keeps
    their results: those are the only answers a read can get.
The app streams its requests; this script does not. Nothing else differs,
except which model answers them.

      [--runs N] [--must-pass N] [--case NAME] [--jobs 5] [--verbose] [--prompt-rev REV]
      [--model NAME [--endpoint URL] [--key-env NAME] [--provider HOST]...]

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""One step of the project chat against the live model, without the app.

The project chat's assistant is a system prompt (projectInstructions.ts), the
project tools and the chat. Each case here is one point in a project chat,
recorded from the real app, and the model's next step there, a tool call or a
reply, checked against one sentence of the prompt. A response may hold
several calls, and every one is judged: a change among them is the outcome
and ends the run, whatever came before it. A response of reads the case does
not decide on is answered, each read with the result the app gave for it at
the same point (recorded beside the request), and the model asked again, at
most MAX_READS times; nothing else is ever answered.

What the app sends, reproduced here:
  - instructions: rendered from projectInstructions.ts by
    tests/printer_prompt/render_prompt.mjs, so an edit to the prompt is tested
    without building anything;
  - tools: project_tools.json, the app's own tool list for the project chat
    (test_openai_responses_agent.cpp fails if it drifts from the registry);
  - input: everything else, as the app built it (requests.json). The shell
    harness's --project-prompt-requests mode plays script.json through the
    real app, with the model's outputs scripted and every tool run for real,
    and keeps the request at each point a case observes: the earlier turns as
    the app replays them, this turn's message with the workspace context, and
    this turn's calls with their live results. At the same point it calls
    the reads script.json's "answers" lists (workspace_inspect, slice_report,
    printer_list, object_analyze for each object, settings_get of every
    setting of the print, the first object, the filament and the printer,
    the filament's and printer's names asked under the print scope, a
    hand-kept list of other slicers' names, and settings_search for common
    queries) and keeps
    their results: those are the only answers a read can get.
The app streams its requests; this script does not. Nothing else differs,
except which model answers them.

def test_reading_rounds_are_capped(self):
        reads = [[call("workspace_inspect")] for _ in range(runner.MAX_READS + 1)]
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", *reads)
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.UNOBSERVED)
        self.assertIn("still reading after answers", detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), runner.MAX_READS + 1)

    # --- A skill is sent on one request ------------------------------------

    def test_a_skill_and_its_picture_leave_the_request_after_theirs(self):
        """The app sends the model-arrived skill and the plate's picture on the
        request that first carries a load report and keeps them out of the
        turn's next request; so does the runner when it answers a read."""
        for name in ("model-opened-unnamed", "model-imported-by-tool", "model-opened-by-tool"):
            recorded = runner.REQUESTS[name]["body"]["input"]
            self.assertEqual(runner.REQUESTS[name].get("once"), 2, name)
            self.assertEqual(recorded[-1]["role"], "developer", name)
            self.assertTrue(recorded[-1]["content"].startswith("# The first message after a model arrives"), name)
            self.assertEqual([part["type"] for part in recorded[-2]["content"]], ["input_image"], name)
            first = [call("workspace_inspect", {}, "call-w")]
            verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case(name, first, [call("plan_set", {"headline": "Print it"})])
            self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL, detail)
            sent = bodies[1]["input"]
            self.assertEqual(sent[:len(recorded) - 2], recorded[:-2], name)
            self.assertEqual(sent[len(recorded) - 2:len(recorded) - 1], first, name)
            self.assertEqual(sent[-1]["call_id"], "call-w", name)
            self.assertNotIn("# The first message after a model arrives", json.dumps(sent), name)
            self.assertNotIn("input_image", json.dumps(sent), name)

    def test_no_other_point_sends_anything_once(self):
        self.assertEqual(sorted(name for name, request in runner.REQUESTS.items() if request.get("once")),
                         ["model-imported-by-tool", "model-opened-by-tool", "model-opened-unnamed"])

    # --- One call or none, as before ---------------------------------------

    def test_a_single_read_then_a_reply(self):
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", [call("workspace_inspect", {}, "call-1")],
                                                [reply("Use 15% gyroid.")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.PASS)
        self.assertEqual(detail, "after workspace_inspect: reply: Use 15% gyroid.")
        self.assertEqual(bodies[1]["input"][-1]["call_id"], "call-1")

    def test_a_single_change(self):
        verdict, detail, _ = self.run_case("advice-infill", [call("slice_start")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertEqual(detail, "CHANGED: slice_start {}")

    def test_a_reply(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.run_case("advice-infill", [reply("Gyroid.")])[:2], (runner.PASS, "reply: Gyroid."))

75:A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
77:## Skills versus tools
79:A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
82:- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
84:The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
86:A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
93:A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists (none does yet). The first skill is `model-opened-or-imported` (trigger `model_arrived`): the first message after a model arrives is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
97:- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
98:- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment

  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur

For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

**Why:** On 2026-09-01 a verification pass screenshotted the stock app instead of the build; on 2026-09-05 the tools bound to another session's main-repo build.

**How to apply:** Confirm the pid with `pgrep -fl OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS`; never kill an instance you did not launch. `osascript` System Events by unix id still works to set `frontmost`. See [[jusprin-shell-phase-1-design]] and [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]].

**"On another Space" usually means "on the other monitor."** Cost about ten turns on
2026-09-09 and produced a wrong report to Kenneth. `app_list_windows` returns
`is_off_space: true` and clicks are refused with "this window is on another Space";
`app_bring_to_current_space` then fails with "the user's current Space is a full-screen
app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it
captured and lists the others — if the window shows up there, it is a monitor problem,
not a Space problem, and the display-scope tools can drive it immediately. Never conclude
"the user is in a full-screen app" from the background tools' error text alone.

The same flag also flaps: a window can read `is_off_space: false` and click fine, then
read `true` a minute later. Clicks delivered while it is true report `ok ... unverified`
and silently do nothing. **A click that reports "unverified" and changes nothing is not
evidence of an application bug** — on 2026-09-09 that nearly became a filed defect about
being unable to retry after a failed MCP connect. Re-verify on a reachable window before
`JusPrinShellHarness --printer-setup` hung forever at
**How to apply:** don't propose a full save as the frequent autosave write or a checkpoint before every agent turn without citing these costs. When re-measuring: the Release harness builds fine; `sample` needs `pgrep -x JusPrinWorkspaceHarness` (plain `pgrep -f` hits the sh wrapper). Heavy Spotlight load on this Mac made the multi-core "many" fixture swing 0.8 s → 47 s; a first 5M-triangle run thrashed memory (3.1 GB footprint, 620 MB resident), so it had to be rerun in a fresh process.
4. Live app without mouse or screen capture: `JusPrinShellHarness` (target
**Recipe.** Start `build/arm64/tests/shell/Release/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --manual-mcp <scratch dir>` with `HOME=<scratch home>`, wait for `HARNESS MCP FIXTURE READY` on stderr (about 15 s), read the URL from `<scratch dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`, then call tools with `probe.call(urlsplit(url), "tools/call", {"name": ..., "arguments": ...})` imported from `tests/mcp/probe.py`. The fixture is two plates, one 20 mm box each, Bambu X1C 0.4, "Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C", "0.20mm Standard @BBL X1C", the same presets as Kenneth's live tests. Another session's harness can run at the same time; the port falls back from 47301 and the discovery file is per data dir.
**Trap 1: leaked harness.** In a script, `cd "$S" && nohup harness ... &` makes `$!` the subshell, so `kill $!` leaves the harness running, and the next run's `rm -rf <fixture>` fails with "Directory not empty". Write `cd "$S"; nohup harness ... &`. Check with `pgrep -fl "<worktree>.*JusPrinShellHarness"` before finishing.
`tests/shell/.../JusPrinShellHarness.app` already carries its own bundle id
- Real app: `JusPrinShellHarness --light-ui|--dark-ui --setup-differences-capture <dir>` edits process, filament, printer and object settings and photographs the web view. Use `capture_web_view` (WebKit snapshot); `write_screen_capture` gives blank 810-byte PNGs from a shell.
Crash reports land in `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/JusPrinShellHarness-*.ips`.

**How to apply:** Confirm the pid with `pgrep -fl OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS`; never kill an instance you did not launch. `osascript` System Events by unix id still works to set `frontmost`. See [[jusprin-shell-phase-1-design]] and [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]].

**"On another Space" usually means "on the other monitor."** Cost about ten turns on
2026-09-09 and produced a wrong report to Kenneth. `app_list_windows` returns
`is_off_space: true` and clicks are refused with "this window is on another Space";
`app_bring_to_current_space` then fails with "the user's current Space is a full-screen
app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it
captured and lists the others — if the window shows up there, it is a monitor problem,
not a Space problem, and the display-scope tools can drive it immediately. Never conclude
"the user is in a full-screen app" from the background tools' error text alone.

The same flag also flaps: a window can read `is_off_space: false` and click fine, then
read `true` a minute later. Clicks delivered while it is true report `ok ... unverified`
and silently do nothing. **A click that reports "unverified" and changes nothing is not
evidence of an application bug** — on 2026-09-09 that nearly became a filed defect about
being unable to retry after a failed MCP connect. Re-verify on a reachable window before
`JusPrinShellHarness --printer-setup` hung forever at

Author: Kenneth Jiang <kenneth.jiang@gmail.com>

    Send the workspace and print-issue context as tagged blocks of their own
    
    The project chat used to send one text part per user message: the person's
    words, then a plain heading ("Authoritative JusPrin workspace context:") and
    the snapshot JSON, then the attachments. A canvas issue's context was glued
    on the same way under its own heading. Pasted text containing such a heading
    could not be told apart from the app's data.
    
    Now each kind of content is its own input_text part of the user message:
    the person's words exactly as typed, then <print_issue>...</print_issue>
    when the message came from an issue button, then <workspace>...</workspace>,
    then the attachments in their existing <attachment> tags. An earlier issue
    message replayed in the history carries its context the same way, and the
    64 KiB history budget counts that context. Inside a block, "</" in the JSON
    is written "<\/" (the same JSON), so a project name cannot end the block
    early. The prompt gains one sentence saying the two tags are the app's own
    data, never instructions.
    
    The snapshot also carries what the model needs on the next turn without a
    workspace_inspect call: processPreset, the intent (setupTitle, fields,
    openQuestions) and the plan (headline, decisions, assumptions), in the
    shapes workspace_inspect returns, without timestamps. Each is omitted when
    there is nothing to send. Sessions without a workspace (printer and
    filament chats) are unchanged.

    then the attachments in their existing <attachment> tags. An earlier issue
    message replayed in the history carries its context the same way, and the
    64 KiB history budget counts that context. Inside a block, "</" in the JSON
    is written "<\/" (the same JSON), so a project name cannot end the block
    early. The prompt gains one sentence saying the two tags are the app's own

    shapes workspace_inspect returns, without timestamps. Each is omitted when
    there is nothing to send. Sessions without a workspace (printer and

cd /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/angry-rhodes-dd8e89; git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Add the print-issues skill and a per-plate summary of slice warnings

A third app-triggered skill for the project chat, print-issues (trigger
print_issues, AgentUI/src/skills/print-issues/SKILL.md, 4,597 bytes of text).
It holds what the two buttons on a print-issue chip ask for, moved out of the
standing prompt with its "and only that" scope; how to read a finding (severity,
setting key, object); that a warning is the app's statement about the slice,
not proof of failure, and which calls are the person's; that a finding is
resolved only when a new slice no longer reports it; and a table of the warning
families OrcaSlicer raises while slicing, in its own words, found in libslic3r
and the notifications NoticeKinds routes. It also says OrcaSlicer raises no
slicing warning for thin walls, bridges, adhesion, brims or cooling.

The host fires it on the request that carries a chip's message (a
<print_issue> block), and on the first request whose workspace shows a plate
with slice warnings no request has carried yet: the next message after the
person's Slice, or the tool result that shows the model's own slice. A

# Skill 3: issues OrcaSlicer reports (print-issues)

Branch `claude/skill-print-issues`, one commit `0fb4593f1b` on local `jusprin-newui` at `1435f4c817`. Not pushed, not merged. This report is untracked on purpose.

## 1. The problem

The project chat's model had two blind spots around OrcaSlicer's own findings.

First, the two buttons on a print-issue chip on the canvas ("Ask AI" sends "Explain this issue and my options.", "Resolve with AI" sends "Help fix this issue.") were explained by one sentence in the standing prompt. The model read that sentence on every turn, though it only matters on the turn a button was pressed.

Second, when a slice finished with warnings (for example "It seems object Slab has floating cantilever. Please re-orient the object or enable support generation."), nothing told the model. The `slice_start` reply looked the same as a clean slice. The model learned of warnings only if it chose to call `slice_report` with its findings section, which is why the prompt says "check slice_report before calling a print ready". If the person pressed Slice themselves, the model was never told at all.

## 2. What changed

**The skill.** A new file, `AgentUI/src/skills/print-issues/SKILL.md`, with trigger `print_issues`. The text is 4,597 bytes; the model-arrived skill is 6,918. It opens with "The rules above still apply" and covers:
- what each chip button asks for, moved out of the prompt with its "and only that" scope;
- how to read a finding: a blocker means no slice or print until it is fixed, a warning means the slice can print. The setting key names what to change, and `settings_search` or `settings_get` says what that setting is. The object narrows where the problem is;
- that a warning is the app's statement about the slice, not proof the print will fail, and which choices belong to the person (support marks, orientation, filament pairing, nozzle);
- that a finding is resolved only when a new slice no longer reports it, not when a setting changes or a chip is closed or ignored;
- a table of the warning families OrcaSlicer raises while slicing, quoting its real messages from `libslic3r` (step warnings, `Print::validate` warnings, slice-result warnings) and the notification kinds `NoticeKinds.cpp` routes. The families are: support needed, empty layers, collisions, path conflicts, paths off the plate, capped motion limits, replaced support patterns, multi-filament and purge, nozzle hardness, and timelapse.

The brief asked for thin walls, bridging, bed adhesion, brims and cooling too. OrcaSlicer raises no slicing warning for any of them, so the skill says so and points to `slice_report`'s sections instead of inventing messages.

**When it fires.** `AgentHost::fire_print_issues` adds the skill as the last item of:
- the request that carries a chip's message (the message has a `<print_issue>` block);
- the first request whose workspace shows a plate with warnings no request has carried yet. After the person's Slice, that is their next message. After the model's own slice, it is the tool result that shows the warnings (the `slice_start` reply when it waited).

A re-slice that reports the same warnings fires nothing. When a slice reports a warning the plate's last slice did not have, it fires again. The skill is never stored, and the next request does not carry it.

**The fact.** Every request now carries each plate's `sliceWarnings` in three places: the `<workspace>` block, a tool result's workspace, and the slicing section of `workspace_inspect` and `slice_start`. It holds the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning to read (critical ones first), in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object. `slice_report` still has the full list.

The workspace adapter reads this from the print-issue monitor through a reader the shell installs. It keeps the summary per plate for as long as that slice is still the plate's current one. It counts the same warnings `slice_report` lists, so it leaves out the bed-temperature warning (code `1000C001`) and a duplicate timelapse warning (`1000C003`). See Remaining issues for why.

**The prompt** loses the print-issue bullet: 2,364 to 2,195 bytes. `workspace_inspect`'s description now mentions the warnings, and `project_tools.json` is regenerated.

**The eval.** `issue-fix` and `issue-explain` are re-pointed to the skill. A new case, `slice-warnings-ready`, covers the overhang fixture sliced by the person, then "is this good to print?". It passes on a `slice_report` read, or on a reply that names the warning as the app's own and recommends what to do. It fails on any change, or on calling the print ready without the warning. The recorder now checks any page skill (`"skill": "print-issues"`), checks that no other point carries a skill, and checks that the next request does not carry it. `requests.json` is re-recorded.

**Size.** 885 lines added and 61 removed, not counting `requests.json`, which has 4,193 lines added and 1,023 removed.

## 3. Tests and results

All of these were run on this branch's final build (Release):

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| `agent_bridge_tests` | 316 cases pass |
| `jusprin_tests` | 113 cases pass |
| `workspace_contract_tests` | 42 cases pass |
| Real-adapter workspace harness | pass, 5,945 checks |
| Shell harness, default scenario | pass, 550 checks |
| Shell harness `--print-issues` | pass, 0 failures |
| AgentUI vitest | 429 tests pass |
| `test_steps.py` | 18 tests pass |
| `run_prompt_tests.py --render-only` | 21 cases render |
| Recorder, `--project-prompt-requests` | pass, 6,724 checks |

The `jusprin_web` bundle was rebuilt before vitest and the recording.

New tests:
- Host tests: the skill on a chip's request, after the person's slice, and after the model's own `slice_start` with wait. Also: no skill on a clean slice, none on any later request, and none for a re-slice with the same warnings. Plus the summary JSON, present and absent.
- PrintIssue tests: which warnings count, the excluded codes, the summary rule, and when warnings count as new.
- Page tests: the skill's content, and that the prompt no longer has the button sentences.

I proved the host tests catch a broken change. With the firing and the summary output disabled, five of them failed; with the code restored, all pass.

In the real app (`--print-issues`), the overhang slice gives "It seems object issues-overhang.stl has floating cantilever…" with its object. The summary is present at the first workspace change that shows the plate sliced. The chip's request carries the skill.

That timing check failed at first, because the monitor had not re-read OrcaSlicer yet. The reader now refreshes the monitor before reading. Its callbacks only redraw the overlay and post chat entries; they never read the workspace.

In the recording, the skill sits on `issue-fix`, `issue-explain` and `slice-warnings-ready`, and on no other point. Before the bed-temperature exclusion, 6 points that should carry nothing carried the skill: every conversation on the Textured PEI Plate had that warning.

I also fixed one existing check in `--print-issues`. `ask_request_gives_the_model_the_structured_context` had been stale since 36d33312ed, which moved the issue context out of the message text into its own block. It would have failed without my change. It now checks the context block and the skill.

## 4. Remaining issues

- **Joining with skill 2 (slice failed).** The sibling's work, branch `claude/skill-slice-failed` in worktree `cool-bardeen-7f40f5`, was uncommitted when I started, so I could not build on it. I matched its shape instead. Its `WorkspacePlate::slice_failure` (a `SliceFailure` with severity, message, setting, code, object, sequence) sits next to my `slice_warnings` (a `SliceWarnings` with the same fields plus count and ignored). Its host side keeps `m_slice_failures_told` beside my `m_slice_warnings_told`, and `fire_on_new_slice_failure` beside `fire_print_issues`. Expect conflicts in these places:
  - `Workspace.hpp`;
  - the plate JSON in `AgentHost::context_json`, `OpenAIResponsesAgent::workspace_json` and `slicing_section_result`;
  - the `slicing_plate` schema;
  - `SkillTrigger`;
  - the same sentence of `workspace_inspect`'s description (merge it to "whether each plate's slice is current, what it warned about and why its last slice did not succeed");
  - `skills.test.ts`'s skill list;
  - the recorder's skill checks: its `prompt_is_any_skill` must also know `slice-failed`.

  A later cleanup could make both records one shared finding type. I left that alone.
- **The prompt's "check slice_report (slice_inspect when needed)".** The warnings part of that sentence is now redundant: the warnings reach the model without a call. The rest is not. The sentence also asks the model to check the slice against the person's requirements (time, weight, cost, supports). I left it for the main session's final prompt edit.
- **The bed-temperature warning is left out.** The chip still shows it, but the summary does not count it, to match `slice_report`, which leaves it out as OrcaSlicer's send dialog does. That means a chip can show a warning the model is not told about. Whether that warning should reach the model is your call.
- **Small edges, not fixed:**
  - If the request that first carries new warnings fails and is retried, the retry does not carry the skill (the warnings already count as told). A chip's retry does carry it.
  - The told list is per app run, not per chat, so a new chat opened after the warnings were told gets the fact but not the skill.
  - Only the active plate is read, because OrcaSlicer checks only the active plate. Another plate keeps what was read while it was active.
- **`first-person`** still starts after the scripted `slice_report`. The skill sits on the request before it, so that case still tests the prompt's first-person rule, not the skill.
- **Proposed live batch (not run).** Cases `issue-fix`, `issue-explain`, `slice-warnings-ready` and `first-person`, 3 runs each: 12 runs. By the README's last comparable batch (12 runs, 35 requests, 398,836 input tokens), expect about 35 requests, roughly 400,000 input tokens (about 70% cached), about 10,000 output tokens, and up to 9 judge calls.

Branch `claude/skill-print-issues`, one commit `0fb4593f1b` on local `jusprin-newui` at `1435f4c817`. Not pushed, not merged. This report is untracked on purpose.

## 1. The problem

The project chat's model had two blind spots around OrcaSlicer's own findings.

First, the two buttons on a print-issue chip on the canvas ("Ask AI" sends "Explain this issue and my options.", "Resolve with AI" sends "Help fix this issue.") were explained by one sentence in the standing prompt. The model read that sentence on every turn, though it only matters on the turn a button was pressed.

Second, when a slice finished with warnings (for example "It seems object Slab has floating cantilever. Please re-orient the object or enable support generation."), nothing told the model. The `slice_start` reply looked the same as a clean slice. The model learned of warnings only if it chose to call `slice_report` with its findings section, which is why the prompt says "check slice_report before calling a print ready". If the person pressed Slice themselves, the model was never told at all.

## 2. What changed

**The skill.** A new file, `AgentUI/src/skills/print-issues/SKILL.md`, with trigger `print_issues`. The text is 4,597 bytes; the model-arrived skill is 6,918. It opens with "The rules above still apply" and covers:
- what each chip button asks for, moved out of the prompt with its "and only that" scope;
- how to read a finding: a blocker means no slice or print until it is fixed, a warning means the slice can print. The setting key names what to change, and `settings_search` or `settings_get` says what that setting is. The object narrows where the problem is;
- that a warning is the app's statement about the slice, not proof the print will fail, and which choices belong to the person (support marks, orientation, filament pairing, nozzle);
- that a finding is resolved only when a new slice no longer reports it, not when a setting changes or a chip is closed or ignored;
- a table of the warning families OrcaSlicer raises while slicing, quoting its real messages from `libslic3r` (step warnings, `Print::validate` warnings, slice-result warnings) and the notification kinds `NoticeKinds.cpp` routes. The families are: support needed, empty layers, collisions, path conflicts, paths off the plate, capped motion limits, replaced support patterns, multi-filament and purge, nozzle hardness, and timelapse.

The brief asked for thin walls, bridging, bed adhesion, brims and cooling too. OrcaSlicer raises no slicing warning for any of them, so the skill says so and points to `slice_report`'s sections instead of inventing messages.

**When it fires.** `AgentHost::fire_print_issues` adds the skill as the last item of:
- the request that carries a chip's message (the message has a `<print_issue>` block);
- the first request whose workspace shows a plate with warnings no request has carried yet. After the person's Slice, that is their next message. After the model's own slice, it is the tool result that shows the warnings (the `slice_start` reply when it waited).

A re-slice that reports the same warnings fires nothing. When a slice reports a warning the plate's last slice did not have, it fires again. The skill is never stored, and the next request does not carry it.

**The fact.** Every request now carries each plate's `sliceWarnings` in three places: the `<workspace>` block, a tool result's workspace, and the slicing section of `workspace_inspect` and `slice_start`. It holds the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning to read (critical ones first), in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object. `slice_report` still has the full list.

The workspace adapter reads this from the print-issue monitor through a reader the shell installs. It keeps the summary per plate for as long as that slice is still the plate's current one. It counts the same warnings `slice_report` lists, so it leaves out the bed-temperature warning (code `1000C001`) and a duplicate timelapse warning (`1000C003`). See Remaining issues for why.

**The prompt** loses the print-issue bullet: 2,364 to 2,195 bytes. `workspace_inspect`'s description now mentions the warnings, and `project_tools.json` is regenerated.

**The eval.** `issue-fix` and `issue-explain` are re-pointed to the skill. A new case, `slice-warnings-ready`, covers the overhang fixture sliced by the person, then "is this good to print?". It passes on a `slice_report` read, or on a reply that names the warning as the app's own and recommends what to do. It fails on any change, or on calling the print ready without the warning. The recorder now checks any page skill (`"skill": "print-issues"`), checks that no other point carries a skill, and checks that the next request does not carry it. `requests.json` is re-recorded.
